Summary: This paper is an Affective Computing dataset comprising functional near Infrared sensor data and EEG data.  The data is 100% free to use on Kaggle and was collected under a protocol that follows established emotion elicitation techniques and uses established instruments such as the self-assessment mannikin and real-time joystick feedback to capture participant experienced emotional response during video elicitation.  Emotion experience is validated three ways: elicitation protocol, real-time user feedback and post-hoc assessment.  Free to use physiological datasets with emotion annotation are uncommon and this would be a valuable resource for researchers in the area to use. 

Scores: (5,5,4) where the lowest rating (which was still positive) did not receive response to the authors rebuttal

Claims:

To the best of our knowledge, no affective BCI dataset simultaneously records multimodal brain signals and provides real-time dynamic emotion annotation.  . We collected multimodal brain signals from 32 healthy participants across emotion-eliciting video clips. By combining EEG and fNIRS, we recorded brain activity from both electrophysiological and hemodynamic perspectives, enabling emotion modeling with high temporal and spatial resolution. Unlike existing affective BCI datasets, our dataset uniquely provides
time-aligned dynamic emotion annotations based on participants’ subjective experiences. 

Claims are true.

Reasons to Accept:

- Well collected physiological dataset of emotional responses with triply validated annotations.
- Free to use by all.

Reasons to Reject:

- Real time dynamic rating may have induced cognitive burden 
- Cognitive assessment of emotion may have influenced emotional response.
- Imperfect specification of all details needed to reproduce, research would have to be familiar with physiological signal processing for the signals in the dataset and be skilled in generating visualizations

We sincerely thank all reviewers and the Area Chair for their thoughtful comments and the opportunity to further clarify our work.

### Summary of contributions:

1. **First publicly available EEG+fNIRS emotion dataset with dynamic annotations** – REFED dataset introduces, to the best of our knowledge, the first publicly available dataset that synchronously records EEG and fNIRS while collecting continuous valence–arousal annotations, enabling richer affective computing and BCI research.
2. **Extensive experimental validation** – We conducted comprehensive analyses to verify the dataset’s reliability and usability. These evaluations span multiple affective recognition tasks and modeling approaches, and include detailed label distribution analyses, visualization-based explorations, as well as supervised learning benchmarks.
3. **Complete and user-friendly dataset structure** – The dataset is well-organized, fully documented, and ready to use, lowering the barrier for researchers to reproduce and extend our results.

### Addressing Reviewer Concerns & Future Improvements:

We have addressed the main concerns raised during the review process in our rebuttal and discussions. In the camera-ready version, we will explicitly integrate the clarifications into the main text, including:

- **Cognitive load from real-time annotation** – We provide an expanded discussion of the potential implications of cognitive load and future mitigation strategies (e.g., hybrid annotation strategies combining self-reports with facial expression).
- **Valence–arousal annotation reliability** – Detailing our standardized participant training procedure, cross-check consistency analysis, and statistical reliability validation, which together confirm annotation quality.
- **Additional baseline models:** We included three updated baseline models to further validate the effectiveness and robustness of our dataset.

In addition, **we will release a complete code repository** to facilitate data loading, preprocessing, and baseline reproduction.

### Closing Acknowledgement:

We remain confident in the novelty, quality, and impact of the proposed REFED dataset, and believe it will make a valuable and lasting contribution to the affective computing and BCI communities. We once again thank the reviewers and AC for their efforts and thoughtful input.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you very much for your recognition of our work and for providing these valuable suggestions. Below are our responses to the key limitations you raised:

> **W1: Cognitive Load from Real-Time Annotation: As acknowledged in Section 6, continuously reporting emotional states using a joystick may distract participants from fully engaging with the emotional stimuli, potentially compromising both the emotional induction and the accuracy of annotations. Although the authors evaluated alternative annotation strategies (e.g., post-hoc recall or facial analysis), no mitigation was implemented in this version of the dataset. Future work could explore hybrid annotation protocols (e.g., combining passive recording with periodic recall) to balance immersion and label quality.**

As acknowledged in our Limitations section, real-time joystick-based annotation may introduce cognitive load, potentially affecting emotional immersion and annotation accuracy. Our initial intention was to collect accurate continuous emotional annotations. However, after evaluating multiple annotation strategies, we found real-time annotation to be the most direct and temporally precise method for capturing participants’ subjective emotional dynamics. Compared to retrospective recall or facial analysis, it offers better alignment with the internal emotional experience. Similar protocols have been adopted in datasets such as CASE and CEAP-360VR, albeit using peripheral signals.

We also considered some mitigation measures to reduce cognitive demands. For example, we provided participants with standardized instructions and ample training, kept video durations reasonable, and included regular rest periods.

We agree that hybrid annotation strategies (e.g., combining periodic self-reports with facial expression) hold promise. A well designed hybrid annotation strategies will improve both the induction effect and annotation quality. However, their implementation may also encounter some problems and increase the burden on test subjects, such as requiring additional time for analysis and correction, which will prolong the collection time and thus more easily lead to test subject fatigue. We plan to explore such methods in future work to better balance emotional immersion and annotation quality for more natural brain–emotion interfaces.

> **W2: Reproducibility and Code Clarity: While the dataset is available on Kaggle and the paper outlines the experimental setup, code and preprocessing documentation are not fully detailed in the main text. For instance, the description of how features were extracted for the SVM models in Section 4.2 and Appendix E is too brief to replicate the benchmarks without guessing key parameters. More comprehensive reproducibility materials (e.g., GitHub repository with scripts, pretrained models) would strengthen usability.**

We fully acknowledge the importance of reproducibility. The complete dataset is already publicly available on Kaggle, and initial experimental details are included in the main text and appendix. Due to the constraints of the rebuttal period, we were unable to release the full codebase. However, upon official publication, we will provide a comprehensive GitHub repository containing preprocessing scripts, feature extraction pipelines, baseline models, pretrained weights, and example notebooks to support easy replication and exploration. Some key technical details include:

- Preprocessing: EEG: bandpass filtering (0.5–50 Hz), notch filtering at 50 Hz, referenced to AFz, resampled to 200 Hz, removed obvious motion artifacts; fNIRS: resampled to 50 Hz for supervised learning tasks, removed obvious motion artifacts; Annotation: regression task uses normalized annotation values; classification task divides the annotations into three categories—high, medium, and low—based on thresholds.
- Feature extraction: EEG – for each channel, extract differential entropy (DE) in 5 frequency bands, to form the feature matrix with dimensions 64 × 5; fNIRS – mean, max, min, std, slope, and DE from 0.01–0.7 Hz , to form the feature matrix with dimensions 51 × 6;
- Data splitting: Apply 3-fold cross-validation for each participant (dividing each participant’s 15 video segments into 3 groups, each containing 1 segment for each of five target emotions. We report the average MAE and MSE across all 32participants finally.
- Environments: Hardware: Intel Core i5-13600K CPU, NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti Super 16GB GPU, 64 GB RAM; Software: Python 3.13.2, Scikit-learn 1.6.1, scipy 1.15.2, mne 1.9.0, PyTorch 2.7.0, CUDA 12.8.
- Model parameters: SVM hyperparameter search over kernel types (linear, rbf, poly) and C values (0.001–100); for MLP and M2NN, we used Adam optimizer with grid search over batch size (16–512) and learning rate (1e-6–1e-2).

We will improve the description of the experimental details in the revised version.

> **W3: Ecological Validity of Emotional Stimuli: Though the video clips were selected from validated databases (Section 3.3), all participants watched the videos in the same fixed order, which could introduce ordering effects or fatigue-related confounds. A randomized or counterbalanced design would be preferable to reduce sequence bias.**

We appreciate your concern regarding potential order effects or fatigue due to fixed video sequencing. Our decision to use a fixed order was based on psychological principles of emotional elicitation. As reported in prior studys, emotional sequences should be carefully designed to avoid carry-over effects and to allow sufficient emotional recovery. As stated in [R1], emotional induction requires a balanced sequence to avoid a particular emotion type always being in the same position, which could lead to cumulative or disruptive sequential effects. [R2] suggests controlling for non-consecutive sequences of similar emotions and inserting neutral segments for emotional recovery. Random order may undermine emotional induction—especially when highly intense emotional clips appear early. Our original intention in using a fixed order was to ensure the effectiveness of emotional induction and consistency in the experience across different participants, which cannot be guaranteed by a completely random order. The consistency between dynamic emotion annotations and the SAM scale demonstrated the effectiveness of our emotion induction.

As for potential fatigue issues, we controlled for fatigue by keeping the total recording session under 40 minutes, limiting clip length, and providing about 30 seconds of rest between clips. Feedback from participants indicated that most found the process easy to operate and did not experience fatigue. Very few participants felt slightly fatigued, but there were no obvious signs of fatigue.

> **Reference:**
>
> [R1] Gross, J. J., & Levenson, R. W. (1995). Emotion elicitation using films. *Cognition & emotion*, *9*(1), 87-108.
>
> [R2] Fernández-Aguilar, L., Ricarte, J., Ros, L., & Latorre, J. M. (2018). Emotional differences in young and older adults: Films as mood induction procedure. *Frontiers in psychology*, *9*, 1110.

We sincerely thank you for your detailed review and constructive feedback.

> **W1: As the authors themselves acknowledge in the limitations, real-time annotation is likely to impose a cognitive burden on the participants.**

We acknowledge that real-time annotation may introduce a certain level of cognitive load. However, based on pilot experiments and participant feedback, we believe this approach currently offers the most reliable and controllable means of collecting dynamic subjective emotion labels. In contrast, retrospective annotation or relying on automated models (e.g., facial expression recognition) often suffers from issues related to accuracy and temporal alignment. Similar real-time annotation methods have been successfully used in existing datasets such as CASE and CEAP-360VR for peripheral physiological signals.

To minimize potential cognitive burden, we provided standardized training and sufficient practice sessions for all participants, and we carefully controlled video durations and the overall session length to prevent fatigue and maintain annotation quality.

> **W2: Even if valence-arousal concepts were well explained to the users, inter-subject variability raises concerns about the dataset’s reliability. (In facial expression datasets, for example, trained annotators are typically employed to ensure fair labeling.)**

We appreciate the concern regarding inter-subject variability in emotion labeling. To address this, we employed both real-time valence–arousal annotations and standardized Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM) scale to assess participants’ emotional states. The questionnaires served as a cross-validation tool for verifying the reliability of real-time annotations.

Recognizing that emotional experience is inherently subjective (for example, everyone has different things that make them laugh or cry), we favor self-reported, participant-centered annotation as it more accurately captures individual differences in affective perception. To ensure consistent understanding of the valence-arousal model, we provided instructional materials before the session, followed by in-person explanations and interactive training using three sample videos. During training, the experimenter monitored annotation trajectories and offered corrections when needed.

We also recorded participants' facial videos (with consent and for internal verification only) to assist in post-hoc validation. Following data collection, additional feedback through questionnaires and interviews further confirmed annotation reliability. The high consistency between participant reports and target emotions supports the robustness of our labeling protocol.

>  **W3: As participants view more videos, their level of concentration may decrease, potentially affecting data quality.**

We fully acknowledge the potential risk of decreased concentration during longer recording sessions. To address this, we carefully structured the experimental procedure to optimize engagement and comfort. The entire session was limited to approximately 40 minutes, with each video lasting around 100 seconds, followed by a 30-second rest and questionnaire period. A 5-second countdown was also presented before each video to help participants refocus.

Based on participant feedback, most reported that the break intervals were sufficient and the session was well-paced. Only a few participants noted minor fatigue, which did not significantly affect their ability to annotate. These results suggest that our design effectively mitigates attention-related issues.

> **W4: The study lacks an ablation analysis of EEG and fNIRS signals, making it difficult to assess the individual contributions and synergy of each modality.**

Thanks for your comment. As detailed in Section 4.2 and Appendix E, we conducted an ablation analysis comparing the performance of EEG and fNIRS both individually and in combination. The results demonstrate that combining both modalities yields superior performance in both classification and regression tasks, highlighting their complementary nature. Furthermore, in Section 4.3, we present visual analyses of key features from each modality, revealing their distinct spatial and temporal contributions to emotion recognition.
From a neuroscience perspective, prior studies have confirmed that the neurovascular coupling mechanism objectively exists [R1, R2], where EEG captures electrical brain activity and fNIRS reflects hemodynamic responses. These two modalities offer non-redundant insights, justifying their integration in our dataset.

> **Reference:**
>
> [R1] Keles, H. O., Barbour, R. L., & Omurtag, A. (2016). Hemodynamic correlates of spontaneous neural activity measured by human whole-head resting state EEG+ fNIRS. *Neuroimage*, *138*, 76-87.
>
> [R2] Yeung, M. K., & Chu, V. W. (2022). Viewing neurovascular coupling through the lens of combined EEG–fNIRS: A systematic review of current methods. *Psychophysiology*, *59*(6), e14054.

We sincerely thank you for your thorough review and insightful comments.

> **W1: As noted in the "Limitations", real-time joystick-based annotation may disrupt emotional immersion and compromise annotation quality. However, its impact on data validity remains unquantified.**

Thank you for your careful attention to our experimental paradigm. As noted in the “Limitations”, real-time annotation may partially interfere with emotional immersion. However, before adopting this method, we systematically compared various continuous annotation paradigms (e.g., retrospective ratings, facial expression assistance), and found that joystick-based annotation offers the best trade-off between temporal resolution and user operability.

To mitigate its potential cognitive impact, all participants underwent standardized instructions and hands-on training to ensure fluent use of the annotation system. Although the exact influence of real-time annotation on data validity is difficult to quantify, as shown in Section 4.1, both the self-report ratings and the dynamic trajectory analyses demonstrate consistent and reliable emotion induction across participants, supporting the effectiveness of our paradigm.

> **W2: The 5-second baseline preceding each video may be insufficient for establishing a stable emotional reference, particularly when switching between emotionally contrasting clips.**

Thank you for raising this important point. The 5-second baseline was designed to establish a neutral emotional reference prior to each video. This duration aligns with the settings of many widely used emotion datasets (e.g., DEAP, AMIGOS), and several others (e.g., SEED, MPED, DREAMER) omit explicit baselines.

Moreover, we incorporated a resting period and a 5-second countdown before each baseline to help participants reset emotionally. On average, participants had over 30 seconds between consecutive videos, which we believe is sufficient for emotional recovery and helps prevent carry-over effects between stimuli.

1. After recruitment, participants received electronic materials explaining the valence-arousal dimension of emotion;
2. At the start of the experiment, the experimenter verbally explained in detail the valence-arousal axes and confirmed comprehension through interactive questioning;
3. A training module consisting of three example videos with different emotional tones was used to help participants familiarize themselves with both the emotion model and real-time annotation system;

rebuttal.value:
Thank you very much for your recognition of our work. Below is our response to your concerns:

> **W1: The real-time joystick-based annotation may impose a high cognitive burden on participants, potentially distracting them from fully experiencing the emotion-eliciting videos and thus impacting both the quality of emotional induction and annotation accuracy.**

We appreciate the insightful concern. Indeed, real-time annotation can introduce a certain level of cognitive load, potentially interfering with the emotional experience. However, we selected the joystick-based continuous annotation method as a practical compromise between annotation precision and participant fatigue. We also considered alternative approaches (e.g., retrospective ratings or voice-based annotations), but these often suffer from temporal inaccuracy and reduced reliability. Therefore, we believe our method currently offers a reasonable balance between ecological validity and data integrity. In future work, we aim to explore more natural and less intrusive annotation paradigms to further reduce participant burden.

> **W2: The experimental setting involved controlled lab environments, EEG-fNIRS caps, and fixed stimulus orders, which may reduce naturalistic emotional expression and introduce order effects.**

**Lab environments and recording devices:** We agree that the laboratory environment, EEG-fNIRS equipment, and other controlled factors may limit the natural expression of emotions. To mitigate these effects, we implemented several measures such as turning off ambient lighting, maintaining stable temperature and humidity, and minimizing the duration of recording sessions. We have also acknowledged these limitations in the manuscript.

Furthermore, bridging the gap between lab-based setups and real-world emotion-aware BCI applications remains a key challenge in the field. We are actively working toward deploying more wearable, user-friendly systems in naturalistic environments to improve ecological validity and broaden the applicability of our work.

**Fixed stimulus orders:** We appreciate the comment on potential order effects introduced by the fixed sequence of stimuli. Random order can indeed eliminate the influence of the emotional sequence effect and prevent emotions from being strongly correlated with the time sequence. Our fixed order was designed based on psychological principles to guide participants through a smoother emotional progression and avoid abrupt emotional shifts, which can reduce the effectiveness of induction and accuracy of annotations. Subjective post-session SAM ratings further confirmed that the fixed sequence effectively elicited the target emotional responses.
We acknowledge that both approaches have advantages and disadvantages, and plan to incorporate partially randomized stimulus orders in future work to evaluate and control for potential order effects.

> **W3: While EEG is sampled at 1000 Hz and fNIRS at ~47 Hz, the emotional annotations are sampled only at 1 Hz, which may be too coarse to capture rapid emotional shifts during high-arousal events. Moreover, encoding the valence–arousal scores as integers in [1, 255] might introduce nonlinearities or discretization artifacts when mapped back to emotional spaces.**

Thanks for your concern regarding the temporal resolution and discretization of emotion annotations. 

**Annotation sampling frequency:** While EEG and fNIRS provide high-resolution physiological data, emotional states typically evolve over several seconds, as supported by prior studies [R1, R2]. Therefore, a 1 Hz annotation rate strikes a practical balance between capturing meaningful emotional dynamics and minimizing participant burden.

**Discretization of annotations:** Regarding the encoding of valence-arousal scores as integers within [1, 255], we acknowledge the potential for discretization artifacts. However, in practice, this resolution has been shown to be sufficient for most affective modeling tasks. Additionally, when applying downstream, there are many solutions available for cleaning and processing annotations to resolve potential nonlinear or discretization issues. Similar encoding strategies have been successfully employed in other continuous annotation datasets such as CASE and CEAP-360VR, which do not record brain signals such as EEG and fNIRS.

> **Reference:** 
>
> [R1] Kreibig, S. D., & Gross, J. J. (2024). Temporal dynamics of positive emotion regulation: Insights from facial electromyography. *Frontiers in Human Neuroscience*, *18*, 1387634.
>
> [R2] Verduyn, P., Delaveau, P., Rotgé, J. Y., Fossati, P., & Van Mechelen, I. (2015). Determinants of emotion duration and underlying psychological and neural mechanisms. *Emotion Review*, *7*(4), 330-335.

summary.value: The paper introduces REFED, a novel multimodal dataset that combines electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recordings with real-time dynamic emotion annotations. Designed for affective brain-computer interface (aBCI) research, REFED includes data from 32 participants who viewed 15 emotion-eliciting video clips, while continuously reporting their emotional states on a valence-arousal coordinate plane using a joystick interface. The dataset offers synchronized neural signals and fine-grained emotional labels at a 1 Hz resolution, enabling both regression and classification tasks. The authors validate the dataset through trajectory analysis, supervised learning benchmarks, and neural activity visualization. REFED is made publicly available via Kaggle and adheres to ethical research standards.

strengths_contributions.value:
The primary strength of this paper lies in its novel integration of EEG and fNIRS brain recordings with real-time, continuous emotion annotations, making REFED the first publicly available dataset to support this combination for affective brain-computer interface (aBCI) research. This enables detailed exploration of neural-hemodynamic coupling during emotional evolution—an area not covered by prior datasets.

Compared to widely used datasets such as DEAP, SEED, DREAMER, and MAHNOB-HCI, which rely solely on EEG and offer static or post-stimulus labels, REFED significantly improves ecological validity by providing 1 Hz dynamic labels captured during emotion elicitation (Section 1–2). It also addresses the limitations of real-time datasets like CASE and CEAP-360VR, which use peripheral signals but lack direct brain measurements (lines 54–58, 104–105).

The dataset is well-structured and clearly documented, covering 32 subjects across five emotion categories (HVHA, HVLA, LVHA, LVLA, MVMA), with detailed experimental protocols (Section 3.1), recording settings (3.2), and emotion annotation strategies (3.5). The paper’s figures—such as the valence-arousal trajectories (Figures 4–5) and activation maps (Figure 7)—are informative and effectively support the claims.

The authors provide baseline supervised learning results (Table 1), demonstrating that combining EEG and fNIRS yields better performance than either modality alone. This validates the utility of REFED for machine learning applications, especially in regression settings that benefit from fine-grained labels.

Presentation-wise, the paper is well-organized and easy to follow, with clearly labeled sections and informative visualizations. The experimental setup is comprehensive, and ethical practices are addressed transparently (Section 5).

Overall, the REFED dataset fills a crucial gap in the aBCI research space, offering a high-impact resource for studying dynamic emotional states through brain signals and for developing more adaptive and temporally precise affective computing models.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
While REFED makes a valuable contribution, several limitations merit consideration:

Cognitive Load from Real-Time Annotation:
As acknowledged in Section 6, continuously reporting emotional states using a joystick may distract participants from fully engaging with the emotional stimuli, potentially compromising both the emotional induction and the accuracy of annotations. Although the authors evaluated alternative annotation strategies (e.g., post-hoc recall or facial analysis), no mitigation was implemented in this version of the dataset. Future work could explore hybrid annotation protocols (e.g., combining passive recording with periodic recall) to balance immersion and label quality.

Reproducibility and Code Clarity:
While the dataset is available on Kaggle and the paper outlines the experimental setup, code and preprocessing documentation are not fully detailed in the main text. For instance, the description of how features were extracted for the SVM models in Section 4.2 and Appendix E is too brief to replicate the benchmarks without guessing key parameters. More comprehensive reproducibility materials (e.g., GitHub repository with scripts, pretrained models) would strengthen usability.

Ecological Validity of Emotional Stimuli:
Though the video clips were selected from validated databases (Section 3.3), all participants watched the videos in the same fixed order, which could introduce ordering effects or fatigue-related confounds. A randomized or counterbalanced design would be preferable to reduce sequence bias.

dataset_code_comments.value:
The dataset is publicly accessible via Kaggle (link provided in Section 5), and the authors note that it follows the CC BY-NC-SA license, which allows for non-commercial use. This open access is commendable and aligns with the goals of the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track.

However, reproducibility is only partially addressed. While the dataset includes raw EEG and fNIRS signals along with 1 Hz dynamic valence-arousal annotations, there is limited guidance on how to:

Preprocess the signals (e.g., filtering, artifact removal, synchronization).

Extract features (e.g., time-frequency, spatial mapping) used in their benchmark models.

Reproduce the reported SVM results in Section 4.2 and Table 1.

No GitHub repository or structured code package is provided for running the supervised learning experiments or reproducing the visualizations (e.g., Figure 6 regression curves, Figure 7 activation maps). There is also no documented pipeline or environment specification for training models, although Appendix E offers some parameter settings.

To improve accessibility and reproducibility, the authors should consider:

Publishing a code repository with data loaders, preprocessing scripts, and benchmark models.

Including Croissant-compatible metadata or a detailed README that describes the file structure and usage examples.

Providing a starter notebook to demonstrate typical usage scenarios such as training a regression model or generating activation maps.

Without these elements, the dataset’s full potential may not be immediately accessible to new users.

The presented paper identifies the following limitations in existing brain-signal-based emotion prediction datasets:
- The use of primarily categorized labels fails to capture fine-grained emotional nuances.
- The dynamic changes in a subject's emotions are often ignored.
To address these issues, the paper proposes REFED:
- The first EEG-fNIRS dataset with real-time dynamic emotional annotations
- Real-time annotations of valence and arousal

strengths_contributions.value: The paper proposes a dataset that more realistically models real-world conditions compared to existing datasets in the field of affective Brain-Computer Interaction (aBCI). It efficiently integrates two modalities available from brain signals and makes a strong effort to capture emotions as they dynamically change in real time (e.g., through the use of valence-arousal (VA) and dynamic labeling). Notably, this is the first such attempt in the aBCI domain, making it a highly commendable contribution.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- As the authors themselves acknowledge in the limitations, real-time annotation is likely to impose a cognitive burden on the participants.
- Even if valence-arousal concepts were well explained to the users, inter-subject variability raises concerns about the dataset’s reliability. (In facial expression datasets, for example, trained annotators are typically employed to ensure fair labeling.)
- As participants view more videos, their level of concentration may decrease, potentially affecting data quality.
- The study lacks an ablation analysis of EEG and fNIRS signals, making it difficult to assess the individual contributions and synergy of each modality.

There is no indication of any unethical practices during data collection, such as the involvement of underage or vulnerable individuals or the infliction of mental or physical distress. Furthermore, the dataset is released strictly for research purposes, which helps prevent potential misuse.

dataset_code_comments.value: The dataset is available on Kaggle and is intuitively organized to make both the data and annotations easy to understand. It provides multiple CSV files that allow for straightforward sorting and exploration. In summary, the dataset is highly accessible, easy to restructure, and well-curated.

additional_feedback.value: Although there are some concerns regarding the reliability and fairness of the data collection process, the authors appear to have done their best within their means. With further experimental validation and theoretical analysis of the dataset, this work has the potential to make a significant contribution to the field.

summary.value:
This paper introduces REFED, the first publicly available emotion dataset that synchronously records EEG and fNIRS brain signals along with real-time dynamic valence-arousal annotations. 32 participants watched 15 emotion-eliciting videos while continuously reporting their emotional states via joystick-based feedback. The dataset captures time-aligned neural and subjective emotional data, enabling fine-grained temporal modeling of affective states.

The authors provide a detailed description of the experimental protocol, recording setup, and annotation system. They validate the dataset through trajectory analysis, neural activation visualization, and supervised learning experiments, demonstrating its utility for emotion recognition and affective brain-computer interface (aBCI) development.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Innovative contribution: First dataset to synchronously record EEG and fNIRS with real-time dynamic emotion annotations.

2. Rigorous design: Includes baseline, video-induced emotions, and SAM ratings to ensure high-quality data.

3. Thorough validation: Dataset quality is supported by visualizations, trajectory analysis, and supervised learning tasks.

4. Open and ethical release: Publicly available, anonymized, and ethically approved, promoting reproducibility.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. As noted in the "Limitations", real-time joystick-based annotation may disrupt emotional immersion and compromise annotation quality. However, its impact on data validity remains unquantified.

2. The 5-second baseline preceding each video may be insufficient for establishing a stable emotional reference, particularly when switching between emotionally contrasting clips.

3. The use of only three baseline models provides a limited scope of evaluation, which may reduce the overall persuasiveness of the empirical validation.

4. Participants may interpret valence and arousal differently. It is unclear whether standardized training was provided to ensure consistent understanding of these emotional dimensions prior to data collection.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

summary.value: The REFED dataset presents the first publicly available multimodal brain-computer interface dataset that synchronously records EEG and fNIRS signals with real-time dynamic emotion annotations based on valence–arousal ratings. Collected from 32 participants across 15 affective video clips, REFED offers high temporal and spatial resolution of brain activity along with 1 Hz emotion trajectories. The dataset enables fine-grained exploration of neural–vascular coupling during emotional evolution and supports both regression and classification tasks in affective computing.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The REFED dataset is the first to combine real-time dynamic emotional annotations with simultaneously recorded EEG and fNIRS signals, addressing a major gap in affective BCI research.
- The use of both EEG and fNIRS offers complementary temporal and spatial resolution, enabling studies on neuro-electrical and hemodynamic responses and their coupling. 
- The dataset introduces real-time joystick-based valence–arousal annotations synchronized with neural data at 1 Hz, allowing more fine-grained temporal modeling.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The real-time joystick-based annotation may impose a high cognitive burden on participants, potentially distracting them from fully experiencing the emotion-eliciting videos and thus impacting both the quality of emotional induction and annotation accuracy
- The experimental setting involved controlled lab environments, EEG-fNIRS caps, and fixed stimulus orders, which may reduce naturalistic emotional expression and introduce order effects.
- While EEG is sampled at 1000 Hz and fNIRS at ~47 Hz, the emotional annotations are sampled only at 1 Hz, which may be too coarse to capture rapid emotional shifts during high-arousal events. Moreover, encoding the valence–arousal scores as integers in [1, 255] might introduce nonlinearities or discretization artifacts when mapped back to emotional spaces.

title.value: REFED: A Subject Real-time Dynamic Labeled EEG-fNIRS Synchronized Recorded Emotion Dataset

abstract.value: Affective brain-computer interfaces (aBCIs) play a crucial role in personalized human–computer interaction and neurofeedback modulation. To develop practical and effective aBCI paradigms and to investigate the spatial-temporal dynamics of brain activity under emotional inducement, portable electroencephalography (EEG) signals have been widely adopted. To further enhance spatial-temporal perception, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has attracted increasing interest in the aBCI field and has been explored in combination with EEG. However, existing datasets typically provide only static fixation labels, overlooking the dynamic changes in subjects' emotions. Notably, some studies have attempted to collect continuously annotated emotional data, but they have recorded only peripheral physiological signals without directly observing brain activity, limiting insight into underlying neural states under different emotions. To address these challenges, we present the Real-time labeled EEG-fNIRS Dataset (REFED). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first EEG-fNIRS dataset with real-time dynamic emotional annotations. REFED simultaneously records brain signals from both EEG and fNIRS modalities while providing continuous, real-time annotations of valence and arousal. The results of the data analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of emotion inducement and the reliability of real-time annotation. This dataset offers the possibility for studying the neurovascular coupling mechanism under emotional evolution and for developing dynamic, robust affective BCIs.
